sittings.bodyEn: A new philosophy graduate is an unlikely founder, and one who attended a conference on doing good effectively came away with a factory-farming idea, plus advice, funding, and a place in an incubator. The charity that followed later reduced the suffering of about a million factory-farmed fish, and went on to spend more than half a million dollars a year. A longer contact list would probably not have produced that, which is the difference between collecting names and joining a community of potential allies. People advised by this guide often say that finding the right room did more for friendship, career progress, and impact than any single tactic, and that it mattered in life as well as work. A group working together can also do more than the same people would do separately. This chapter is about why that happens and how to get into a room that fits.

terms.hook: If they say this, they mean a group of potential allies, from a few friends to a movement with events.

sittings.bodyEn: Good professional communities, from startup batches to academic scenes, boost a career partly because connections bring jobs, current information, and motivation. They go further than a contact list because people can specialise: a software product is better built by a designer, an engineer, and a marketer than by one person learning all three badly. The team also shares fixed costs, such as registration and routines, and raising three times the money is not three times as hard, which is a gain from scale. Together that is gains from trade: three people can produce more than three times what one person produces alone, even after they split the results. Helping works the same way when each person goes deep on one piece instead of everyone attempting the whole job. You can trade even with someone who rejects your cause, as when an animal-welfare organiser and a global-health organiser each know a donor the other needs, so two small introductions can create two large gifts. A room that wants the same outcome is stronger still, which is why the choice of group matters more than the size of the contact list.

terms.hook: If they say this, they mean a group producing more by specialising and sharing costs.

sittings.bodyEn: The people you see most often set what feels normal, so generous company makes generosity ordinary, and company that bends the truth makes dishonesty feel acceptable. Every community has its own culture, so try several and go deeper in the ones that support you, ideally more than one. Spending time in several rooms keeps your identity from depending on a single set of ideas, which is how a group becomes an echo chamber that is hard to question. A community here can be a few friends, a reading group, or a chat, not only a branded network with conferences. Start from the people you want around you, and if that group does not exist, you can assemble a small one yourself. Ideas can come from a problem you want to work on, such as biological risk or industrial animal farming, from a craft such as research, writing, or starting things, from a broader political scene, or from a practice group built around honest communication, clearer thinking, or a faith that trains character. The effective-altruism community is one more option, and the chapter counts itself as part of it.

terms.hook: If they say this, they mean one group whose views become hard to question.

sittings.bodyEn: Effective altruism, as this chapter describes it, is the effort to discover better ways to help, for example by preferring problems that are huge, little worked on, and actually movable. It is both a research effort that tries to rank urgent problems and the responses that actually work, and a practical community that tries to act on those findings, and this project was among the groups that helped start it. The four values it lists are a stricter ranking of what actually helps, a wider and more equal concern for others, a harder look at your own views, and cooperation that keeps its standards. Sharing those values, and actively searching for help that works better, is enough to count as taking part, and it is a reason to meet the others who are doing that work. People who have also been inside famous scholarships, business schools, and global forums often say the conversations here are more useful, partly because the people are unusually strong. The other reason is neglect: if you work on issues most networks ignore, and if you compare options by impact more strictly than is normal, you will not find many collaborators in conventional rooms.

terms.hook: If they say this, they mean the project of finding better ways to help.

sittings.bodyEn: Cooperation does not require matching values, because a swap can still leave both people ahead, and matching aims removes even the need for a swap. Here the common goal is more effective help, so raising someone else's contribution already raises yours, and you do not need a returned favour to come out ahead. That opens more joint work than a room where everyone is keeping score. One early split was between running this organisation and earning to fund it: the person with higher earning potential became an early donor, including to other groups, and the person better suited to run it became the director, which beat both of them earning or both of them staffing the same organisation. Across the community, the same logic says the people best at earning can fund the people best at running the work. Others can explore a new area and report back so everyone else is more effective later, or specialise so that nobody has to be a generalist. A doctor who found that clinical work saved fewer lives than he had thought trained in public health to cover pandemics for the community, even though he thought AI risk might be more urgent overall, because medicine was where he had a relative advantage.

terms.hook: If they say this, they mean helping someone who wants the same outcome already counts as impact.

sittings.bodyEn: The same community attracts unusual people, and agreeing with the values does not mean you will like the culture you actually meet. Some readers find the focus on impact totalising, and others dislike how tight the network feels, or other parts of the culture. The chapter's advice is to try more than one group, then reduce involvement if it is not supportive, which is easier if you have kept a foot in other communities. There has also been serious controversy, especially after the collapse of FTX, which led many people to question the organisations, the culture, and the underlying ethos. The chapter points to public critiques, including a general encyclopedia page and the project's own list of common objections, rather than waving the criticism off. If this guide matched how you want to help, you will probably share aims with many people in the community, and the resources for getting involved sit in a later appendix.

The chapter does not send everyone into one network, and the test for any community is whether you can learn there and work with the people. It generally recommends a community built around the global problem you care about. That might be AI alignment, animal welfare, biosecurity, the more evidence-focused side of global health, or the international-relations circles that work on nuclear war and great-power conflict. Academic fields have their own conferences, and a professor can usually name the ones worth attending if you are starting out or still in school. Many readers also overlap with the rationality community, whose online hub named here is LessWrong. The chapter knows these other rooms less well, and it still treats them as real options beside the one it belongs to.

Before the one-minute summary, the chapter asks you to picture the end of a career of about eighty thousand hours. The regrets it wants you to take seriously are drifting into whatever was easiest, copying what a parent did, or earning a comfortable life and still wondering what it was for. The contrast is a life of hard work that saved the lives of a hundred children, which would be difficult to look back on as a waste. Fulfilment, in this close, comes from turning outward. The better question is how you can contribute, not what your passion is. Using a fortunate position with some strategy can help other people a great deal, often at a small cost to you, and often inside a career that is more successful and more satisfying as well.

A good career, in this close, comes from contributing, and fulfilment grows as you learn your fit and master useful skills rather than from a sudden discovery of passion. Explore until a longer option is worth a real bet, by testing your uncertainties instead of following a gut feeling or cutting the list too early. Then build capital, meaning skills, reputation, connections, and character that speed you toward that vision, until the best chances to invest in yourself have been used. Then deploy that capital on problems that are large, neglected, and solvable, rather than on whatever problem you happen to stumble into. Compare earning to give, research, communication, community building, organisation building, government and policy, and direct helping, choose by personal fit, stay ambitious because the best attempts can be enormous even though many fail, and remember that a large impact is possible inside an ordinary job too. Keep revising like someone testing a hypothesis, with a loose longer vision and much more attention on the next step, working both backward from the vision and forward from openings in front of you, and drop any job that does significant direct harm even when it looks like a route to more impact later. The picture of working together is preventing another pandemic, reducing the risks from AI, and ending extreme poverty and factory farming, inside lives that are also interesting, and the hours of a career are the budget you can still waste.

terms.hook: If they say this, they mean significant harm, which rules a job out even if it looks useful later.

sittings.bodyEn: If you still need a plan, the chapter points to a worksheet that collects the exercises from the guide. If the guide was useful, there is a simple way to send a free copy to someone else who is in the middle of choosing. The pages after this chapter are not a new argument: further articles on the main ideas, summaries of the career reviews, and summaries of the top problem profiles. An advanced series sits beyond those summaries if you want to keep reading. The practical close is to make the plan, then use a community so the contribution is shared rather than carried alone.

A community is a set of potential allies, and the gains come from specialisation and shared costs, not from the length of a contact list. You can still trade with people who reject your cause, and when aims match, helping someone else succeed already counts. The norms of the room become what feels ordinary, so spend real time in more than one community and step back if a group is not supportive. The one-minute close of the whole guide is to explore, then build capital, then deploy it on problems that are large, neglected, and solvable. Choose among earning to give, research, communication, community building, organisation building, government and policy, and direct help by personal fit. Refuse work that does significant direct harm even when it looks like a shortcut to a larger impact later.

You should join only one group and adopt every view in it
Allies can specialise and share costs, and shared aims make helping someone else already valuable
Communities matter only when everyone already has the same job title
